title: MB7-25366
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): This is an appeal filed by XXXX XXXX XXXX against a decision rendered by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on December 4, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: This is an appeal filed by XXXX XXXX XXXX against a decision rendered by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on December 4, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
The appellant is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the panel's determination and to grant her refugee status.

The appellant is not asking to submit new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA) and she has not requested an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
The Minister's representative did not intervene in the appeal.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.
According to the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant is a citizen of Chad, born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
In her account, she alleges that she was forced to enter into a marriage imposed by her father. Her father wanted to give her in marriage to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in July 2016.

On August 16, 2016, the appellant's father assembled the marabouts in the mosque and they performed the fatiha. The marriage was planned for October 15, 2016, the day she was to move into her husband's house.
The appellant confided in her brother, who helped her obtain a visa for the United States and hid her with a friend.
The appellant left her country on XXXX XXXX or XXXX for the United States, and later lived with someone in Washington named XXXX, who helped her reach the Canadian border on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

The panel notes that, according to the interview at the Saint-Bernard de Lacolle border crossing, the appellant was married by force on May 1, 2016, to someone other than the person named in her account, and that her mother died on May 3, 2016, whereas according to the account she submitted, her mother died on October 4 of that year. The residence permit was obtained with her mother's help, and the visa was obtained through a cousin who enrolled her in college in Washington. Lastly, her issues began in October 2016, according to her testimony.
The RPD rejected the appellant's refugee protection claim after determining that she is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, owing to a lack of credibility.

The appellant argues that the RPD's determination should be set aside and the appeal allowed. She adds that the decision contains numerous errors in the assessment of her credibility and fails to consider the other aspects of the claim.
For questions of fact, law, and mixed fact and law, the RAD applied the correctness standard set out in Huruglica.2

I conducted an independent analysis of all evidence on the record after listening carefully to the recording of the hearing, in order to form my own opinion about this claim for refugee protection and to determine whether the decision rendered by the RPD is correct.
After reviewing all of the testimonial and documentary evidence on the record, the RAD arrives at the same conclusion as the RPD, that the appellant is not credible.

The appellant is of the view that the RPD failed to adequately assess the marriage and the time spent with her spouse. She also states that her testimony was ignored. The RPD states in its decision that everything about the marriage is confusing, including the date of the marriage and when they moved in together, as well as the document submitted, Exhibit P-4, which contradicts some of the testimony heard.

The appellant states in her memorandum that the marriage took place on August 16, 2016, and that on October 15, there was a celebration and the bride went to live with her husband. The RPD noted that the appellant moved in with her husband approximately five weeks after she was taken to his home by force on October 15.

In her testimony, the appellant stated that the marriage, or the wedding, which is the same thing, was planned for October 15. She also stated that the marriage was held on August 16 and that October 15 was the wedding day. This convoluted situation made her testimony arduous and, at times, contradictory.

The appellant filed an important exhibit, namely, the marriage certificate (Exhibit P-4) which indicates that the marriage was held on October 15, 2016. When confronted with her own document, she testified that she [translation] "did not read it all...and does not know the content of the document." She states indicates in her memorandum [translation] "that it is not an important document for the appellant." If that is the case, why file the exhibit if it has no use?

The appellant does not know the witnesses who signed the marriage document. Other than this information, which is useful to say the least, she did not notice that her future spouse was single according to the document, even though she alleges that he has three wives (she is apparently the fourth) and an unknown number of children. What is more, October 15, 2016, is the date of the document establishing the union between the two individuals, as in the account provided in the Personal Information Form that was confirmed at the start of the hearing as being true and correct, where the appellant states in her account that she was married on October 15, 2016.

All of this confusion surrounding an important life event that is central to the claim for refugee protection undermines the appellant's credibility. Even conceding that there are two steps in a marriage in Chad, the appellant gave dates and then stated the opposite. Moreover, a document she filed that was issued by the civil status centre adds more information that contradicts her testimony.

The RAD is of the view that the testimony concerning this marriage is, at the very least, confusing and contradicts the exhibits submitted and the account filed. Lastly, the appellant was unable to explain the contradictions raised during the hearing, which undermines her credibility on the issue that is central to her claim for refugee protection.

The statement in the memorandum that the testimony was confusing and that it was disregarded solely because the panel did not understand the objective situation does not hold up. The appellant herself led the first-level decision-maker astray and got lost in her explanations.

The final point raised in the memorandum pertains to a handwritten document found in the appellant's luggage when she arrived at the border crossing. The text, on a loose sheet of paper, contains information for which she was able to give the first panel a satisfactory explanation. She stated that she had not received this document and needed a postponement to review it. The RPD was surprised by this situation, and considering the brief one-page handwritten document, refused to grant a postponement. The situation arose at the start of the hearing, as the appellant had not submitted exhibits according to the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada's rules of practice.

The appellant testified that she did not know where this sheet of paper came from and that it did not concern her. She states in her memorandum that someone had given her the information but that she did not use it. Then, she stated that her landlady in Washington, XXXX, was trying to help her. [translation] "She wrote these words for me so that I could say them when I arrived here." The panel must note that a sheet was found randomly among her personal effects, and that she had never discussed her problems with XXXX, yet this information is consistent with a version of an account the appellant submitted concerning a man, a marriage date and the date of her mother's death, which are contrary to the information in the BOC Form. The panel notes that these points are reiterated in her account, but with different information. The appellant was unable to explain why and how this sheet came to be in her bag and what impact it might have on her account or in her life recently.
Consequently, the RAD is of the view that the RPD did not err in its analysis of this document and the appellant's convoluted testimony on this subject.
For the foregoing reasons, the RAD is of the view that the RPD rendered the appropriate, correct decision.

For these reasons, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor "a person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
